stem: Restriction endonucleases, such as EcoRI, are enzymes that
options: cut DNA at specific base sequences
join broken DNA fragments together end to end
copy RNA into DNA
unwind the DNA double helix
explanation: Each restriction enzyme recognises a particular short sequence (EcoRI recognises GAATTC) and cuts DNA only there. Joining fragments is the work of DNA ligase, which is the common mix-up.

stem: In making recombinant DNA, the gene and the plasmid are cut with the same restriction enzyme so that
options: the plasmid loses all its genes
they have matching sticky ends that can base-pair
the gene is copied many times at once inside the tube
no DNA ligase is needed afterwards
explanation: Enzymes such as EcoRI make staggered cuts, leaving short single-stranded ends; ends made by the same enzyme are complementary and pair up. DNA ligase is still needed to seal the sugar-phosphate backbone.

stem: The small circular DNA molecules of bacteria, widely used as vectors in genetic engineering, are called
options: chromosomes
ribosomes
plasmids
mesosomes
explanation: Plasmids replicate independently of the bacterial chromosome and often carry antibiotic-resistance genes, which help identify cells that took them up. Mesosomes are infoldings of the bacterial membrane, not DNA.

stem: The DNA polymerase used in the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) comes from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus because it
options: works only at low temperatures
does not need any primers
cuts DNA at specific sites
is not destroyed at the high temperature used to separate DNA strands
explanation: Each PCR cycle heats DNA to about 95 °C to separate the strands; Taq polymerase from this hot-spring bacterium survives that heat, so fresh enzyme need not be added every cycle. Like other DNA polymerases it still needs primers.

stem: Starting from one double-stranded DNA molecule, the number of copies of the target DNA after 5 cycles of PCR, assuming perfect doubling, is
explanation: Each cycle doubles the number of molecules, so after n cycles there are 2ⁿ copies: 2⁵ = 32. 10 assumes two copies are added per cycle, and 64 is 2⁶, one cycle too many.

stem: The first approved human gene therapy, in 1990, treated a girl with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) by
options: giving her regular injections of antibiotics
inserting a normal ADA gene into her white blood cells and returning them to her body
replacing all her red blood cells with donor cells
removing the faulty gene from every cell in her body
explanation: Her T lymphocytes were taken out, given a working copy of the adenosine deaminase gene with a viral vector, and infused back. Gene therapy adds a working gene to some cells; it cannot remove a faulty gene from every cell.

stem: Dolly the sheep was cloned by
options: fertilising an egg with two sperms
splitting an early embryo into two halves
injecting a human gene into a fertilised egg
transferring the nucleus of an udder cell into an egg whose nucleus had been removed
explanation: In somatic cell nuclear transfer, the nucleus from an adult mammary (udder) cell was put into an enucleated egg, which developed into an embryo and was implanted in a surrogate mother. So Dolly was genetically identical to the udder-cell donor, not to the egg donor.

stem: Human insulin for diabetic patients is now produced on a large scale by
options: genetically modified bacteria carrying the human insulin gene
extracting it from the pancreas of cattle
chemical synthesis from glucose
culturing human liver cells
explanation: The human insulin gene is inserted into plasmids and put into bacteria such as E. coli, which then make human insulin. Animal insulin from cattle or pigs was used earlier but differs slightly from human insulin.

stem: Bt cotton is resistant to some insect pests because it carries a gene from Bacillus thuringiensis that codes for
options: an enzyme that fixes nitrogen
a protein that makes leaves taste sweet
a protein toxic to insect larvae
a hormone that speeds up flowering
explanation: The Bt gene produces a crystal (Cry) protein that is harmless to humans but kills insect larvae such as bollworms after they eat the plant. This reduces the need for chemical insecticide sprays.

stem: The idea that characteristics acquired during an organism's lifetime, through use and disuse of organs, are passed to its offspring was proposed by
options: Darwin
Lamarck
Mendel
Wallace
explanation: Lamarck's theory of inheritance of acquired characteristics claimed, for example, that giraffes got long necks by stretching. Darwin and Wallace proposed natural selection, and Mendel studied the laws of inheritance.

stem: According to Darwin's theory, new species arise mainly because
options: natural selection favours individuals with useful inherited variations
organisms change their bodies by use and disuse
all offspring survive and reproduce equally
mutations occur only when they are needed
explanation: More offspring are produced than can survive; individuals with favourable heritable variations survive and reproduce more, so these traits spread over generations. Change by use and disuse is Lamarck's view, and mutations occur randomly, not on demand.

stem: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 9 % of individuals show a recessive trait (aa). The percentage of heterozygous carriers (Aa) is
explanation: q² = 0.09, so q = 0.3 and p = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7; carriers are 2pq = 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42, i.e. 42 %. 21 % forgets the factor 2, and 49 % is p², the homozygous dominant fraction.

stem: The forelimbs of a human, a whale and a bat look different and have different uses, but have the same basic bone pattern. They are
options: homologous organs, showing common ancestry
analogous organs, showing convergent evolution
vestigial organs with no function
the result of acquired characteristics
explanation: Homologous organs share the same basic structure and embryonic origin but may serve different functions, pointing to a common ancestor (divergent evolution). Analogous organs, such as the wings of insects and birds, do the same job but have different structures.
